items.title: Atom Computing Finalizes $100 Million U.S. Department of Commerce R&D Award
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Atom Computing signed an agreement for up to $100 million with the U.S. Department of Commerce to accelerate development of fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum computers.

The funding will support in-house technology development, expanded engineering and testing infrastructure, and collaboration with supply chain partners.

Atom Computing also advanced to Stage C of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, with potential funding of up to $300 million.

PRESS RELEASE — Atom Computing , a leader in scalable neutral-atom quantum computing, today announced it has signed an agreement for up to $100 million with the U.S. Department of Commerc e to accelerate research and development of fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum computers. The award follows a Letter of Intent announced earlier this year and represents a significant investment in advancing next-generation computing technologies critical to U.S. economic competitiveness, scientific leadership, and national security.

Atom Computing ‘s neutral-atom architecture is increasingly recognized as one of the most viable approaches for building large-scale, commercially useful quantum computers. Today’s announcement closely follows the company’s recent selection as the only neutral atom company to advance to Stage C of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (DARPA QBI) with potential funding up to $300 million.

Atom has consistently demonstrated technical leadership through several industry milestones, including being the first to build a platform with more than 1,000 qubits, the first neutral-atom company to demonstrate sub-threshold behavior on a system with full, end-to-end quantum error correction over many rounds, and the first to commercially offer a logical-qubit quantum computer. In 2025 Atom Computing sold its first commercial on-premises quantum computer to QuNorth, a Nordic quantum initiative funded by EIFO and Novo Nordisk Foundation.

items.title: U.S. Quantum Ambitions Face a Supply Chain Test, Policy Analysts Warn
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Analysts at the Foundation for American Innovation recommend coordinated U.S. investment in quantum components and manufacturing capacity to support commercialization and reduce supply chain vulnerabilities.

The analysis identifies limited access to essential inputs, competition from AI infrastructure demand, fragmented government coordination and unstable federal funding as key obstacles.

Recommendations include advance purchase commitments, targeted manufacturing investments, shared supply chain information and clearer federal plans to buy quantum computing systems.

Image: Photo by Karine Avetisyan on Unsplash

U.S. quantum ambitions could outpace the supply chains needed to turn laboratory advances into a commercial industry, four policy analysts warn.

In a policy piece published by the Foundation for American Innovation , Joshua Levine , Prineha Narang , Jacqueline Tame and Alexandra Seymour Gabel , write that Washington must invest in the components and manufacturing capacity behind quantum technologies while supporting efforts to build useful machines.

items.title: Release v5.23.0
items.summary:
Release v5.23.0

New Model additions

Inkling2

Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs, and it is intended for use in English and other languages and across multiple coding languages. Its language backbone has 48 mixture-of-experts decoder layers, each routing tokens to 8 of 384 experts, for 594B total and 17B active parameters. It keeps the Inkling decoder (learned relative attention, short causal convolutions, mixture-of-experts layers) and adds block attention residuals, gated attention with a learned sink, and dynamic key/value convolutions. Images are encoded by a Perception Encoder-based vision transformer and projected into the language model embeddings, one embedding per 40x40 pixel patch.

items.title: The Geometry of Quantum Memory: How Anyons Rewrite the Rules of Remembering and Computation in the Quantum Realm
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Topological quantum computing aims to store quantum information in a system’s global, topological properties. There, local noise cannot reach it, potentially cutting the large qubit overhead that conventional error correction demands.

Anyons are quasiparticles that emerged from the theoretical work of Jon Magne Leinaas and Jan Myrheim (1977), and Frank Wilczek (1982). They gained a physical home in the fractional quantum Hall effect, and Alexei Kitaev tied them to computing in 1997.

Experiments directly observed Abelian anyons in 2020. But, researchers have yet to conclusively observe, in a real material, the non-Abelian anyons needed for computation by braiding. This makes their search one of the field’s most ambitious bets.

An ordinary qubit remembers too much and listens too well. Its delicate phase is the hidden part of a qubit’s state. It carries much of the qubit’s information and is very easy to disturb. The phase takes account of every stray field, lattice vibration, and fluctuating charge. In turn, a qubit lives a fragile existence and decoheres due to unwanted interactions with its environment.

But what if we could curb a qubit’s ability to listen to the environment, giving it a selective “amnesia”? What if a qubit could store information somewhere local disturbances cannot see? And what if its operations depended on how particles are tangled, rather than exactly how they move?

This is the core idea behind topological quantum computation and it all begins with the two-dimensional loophole that brings to life the strange particles at its heart.

items.title: Ensemble phase transitions in measurement-unitary hybrid quantum circuits
items.summary:
The universal properties of state ensembles generated by quantum dynamics provide a refined lens into Hilbert-space ergodicity and deep thermalisation, or lack thereof. We investigate deep-ergodicity breaking transitions of an ancillary qubit entangled with a system undergoing dynamics via hybrid quantum circuits, where unitary evolution is interspersed with projective measurements.

Specifically, we analyse the statistical properties of two distinct state ensembles: the trajectory ensemble (TE) conditioned on the measurement outcomes of the hybrid circuit, and the projected ensemble (PE) generated by further projective measurements of the system at the final temporal boundary. We find that both ensembles undergo non-analytic changes -- ensemble phase transitions -- at the critical point of the measurement-induced purification transition, despite their first moments remaining completely maximally mixed and blind to the transition.

For Haar-random circuits, the TE transitions from a trivial identity ensemble to the uniform Haar ensemble, while the PE transitions from the Haar ensemble to a trivial singleton pure state. In Clifford circuits, absence of non-stabiliserness limits the PE to a $1$-design, while the TE forms a $k$-design for $k \leq 3$.

We demonstrate that these genuine ensemble transitions offer a clear physical mechanism for the measurement-induced entanglement or purification transitions, illustrating how the capacity to ergodically steer a quantum subsystem shifts from the temporal boundary measurements in the mixed phase to the bulk trajectory measurements in the pure phase.

items.title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate
items.summary:
Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps.

Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer.

Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$.

It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.

items.title: Observation of Genuine Multi-Time Quantum Memory
items.summary:
Memory effects in open quantum systems do not by themselves imply quantum memory, since non-Markovian dynamics can often be reproduced by classical-memory models. Known criteria certify the presence of quantum memory in the environment by comparing the evolution of the system at two different times.

We show that quantum memory can remain hidden from all such pairwise tests and become detectable only when three or more times are considered jointly. We derive an analytical three-time witness and use it to certify quantum memory in a minimal qubit example in which every pair of times has a classical-memory explanation, thus establishing a strict hierarchy of quantum memory effects.

Genuine multi-time quantum memory does not rely on fine-tuned time-dependent Hamiltonians or gate-based evolution. We experimentally demonstrate the hierarchy of quantum memory in a time-continuous realization on a superconducting-qubit platform with time-independent couplings.

items.title: A deployed four-city entanglement-based QKD network with real-time key delivery, benchmarked against finite-key security bounds
items.summary:
Quantum key distribution (QKD) generates shared secret keys whose security rests on the laws of physics rather than on computational assumptions. We report the entanglement-based segment of the Slovak national quantum communication infrastructure, connecting four cities in western Slovakia over deployed telecommunication fiber.

Polarization-entangled photons generated at a central node are passively routed by wavelength to form a trusted-node-free, fully meshed sub-network of three cities, with the fourth connected through the central node and all links operated simultaneously. We also introduce a matrix formalism for passive wavelength routing that enables the algorithmic construction of uniquely and fully connected topologies.

Unlike most previous demonstrations, which estimate key rates from raw coincidences, all rates reported here are obtained after the complete post-processing chain, with keys delivered in real time via ETSI GS QKD 014. With partial non-local chromatic dispersion compensation, we obtain 13.5 bit/s over 109 km, and 4.3 bit/s over 32.1 dB of accumulated loss between two cities without a direct fiber link.

Benchmarking against finite-key security bounds shows that the implemented heuristic privacy amplification can exceed the finite-key bound, and that replacing detect-and-discard with error correction would increase the finite-key rate by a factor of 4.1-6.6, and yield a positive finite-key rate on the 142.9 km link where the implemented scheme yields none.

items.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
items.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear.

Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems.

For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference.

We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm.

These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

items.title: Train the Trainer: Inside MAHE’s Hardware-First Bet on Quantum
items.summary:
Through its partnership with QuantrolOx, Manipal Academy of Higher Education is preparing educators like Dr. Chandrakantha Bekal to run a live quantum facility.

Insider Brief

India’s quantum ambitions are moving from theory and software toward physical systems, and the limiting factor is people who can operate the hardware. As domestic startups and projects like the upcoming IBM Quantum System Two in Amaravati bring real machines online, the country needs an on-the-ground workforce that its software-heavy education system hasn’t produced.

Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE), through an MoA with QuantrolOx, has set up Q-Hub@MAHE on the open-architecture VIDYAQAR platform, which lets the university choose its own QPUs, electronics and dilution refrigerators. It paired the facility with the Quantum EDGE Academy, a simulator-style training environment.

With its dilution refrigerator installed and the facility ready for live experiments, MAHE is now focused on running the system reliably and building local troubleshooting skills. Over a 3-to-5-year horizon, the university aims to establish a fully operational quantum hub and a home-grown, hardware-literate workforce, starting with first- and second-year undergraduates.

For Chandrakantha Bekal, teaching had never been a lifelong interest. After completing his master’s degree in product design and manufacturing, Bekal stepped into the hustle and bustle of job hunting in India, seeking a position in the engineering industry. But life had a different plan.

After positive client feedback on his teaching skills, Bekal spent a few years in the educational sector, assisting various clientele and students alike. This unexpected spark became a consistent thread of interest. ​In 2018, Bekal completed his doctoral degree in computational biomechanics at the Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE) and then moved through various teaching roles within the School of Mechanical Engineering, gaining valuable research and teaching experience within the MAHE ecosystem. ​Yet Bekal couldn’t shake the feeling that something was missing.

items.title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
items.summary:
State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order.

We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow.

Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers.

This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.

items.title: Multi-particle quantum walk search on a two-dimensional lattice
items.summary:
In the present paper we study the formulation of a search problem and the efficiency of multi-particle quantum walk search algorithms. The discrete-time evolution of each particle in space is treated according to Grover's quantum walk evolution operator.

We focus on the local interactions models, where the particles' states are modified only when two or more of them appear on the same grid site. The main focus is given to the two-dimensional grid in space.

We study the dependence of the search algorithm asymptotic success time and probability on the interaction strength and the generated maximal entanglement between particles. We show that the interacting and non-interacting two- and three-particle search algorithm attains a constant factor improvement over the single-particle counterpart.

In addition, we provide a new generalized model of interactions for multi-particle quantum walks.

items.title: Haiqu Appoints Kortny Rolston-Duce to Lead Ecosystem Development and Marketing
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Haiqu has appointed Kortny Rolston-Duce as head of ecosystem development and marketing to lead brand development and expand access to its quantum software.

Rolston-Duce joins Haiqu from Quantinuum, where she served as director of ecosystem development and built partnerships across government, academia and industry.

Her appointment comes as Haiqu expands its AI-enabled software portfolio, including HaiquOS, which translates natural-language problem descriptions into quantum algorithms, and AgenticOS, a multi-agent system for quantum research workflows.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum AI software developer Haiqu today announced the appointment of Kortny Rolston-Duce as head of ecosystem development and marketing. In her new role, she will build the Haiqu brand and work to put its software in the hands of researchers in academia, government labs and companies interested in using quantum computers.

A recognized leader in the quantum computing industry, Rolston-Duce brings extensive experience building partnerships across government, academia and commercial industries, as well as deep expertise in marketing emerging technologies. She joins Haiqu as the company expands its portfolio of AI-enabled software designed to help scientists and domain experts use today’s quantum computers.

“Our first priority was building software that makes today’s quantum computers useful. Now we’re focused on getting those tools into the hands of the people who can put them to work,” said Richard Givhan, Haiqu CEO. “Kortny understands both the technology and the research community. She has built the relationships that help turn emerging quantum capabilities into meaningful scientific opportunities. That experience makes her an ideal leader for our next stage of growth.”

items.title: Entanglement detection from moments of the realigned state: application to continuous-variable quantum systems
items.summary:
Certifying entanglement is a central problem in quantum information sciences, especially for continuous-variable quantum systems where full state tomography is experimentally demanding. We introduce a family of separability criteria based on the singular moments and weak moments of the operator obtained by applying the realignment map to the density operator.

In practice, we find that the criterion based on the second-order moments of the realigned operator is already sufficient to witness the entanglement of a wide range of quantum optical states. The realigned moments can be readily accessed using an optical scheme consisting of a linear interferometer that couples several identical copies of the state, similarly to the multicopy technique used to measure the partial-transpose moments of a state [Phys.

Rev. Research 8, 033064 (2026)].

We illustrate the detection capability of the second-order realigned-moment method for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, including lossy NOON states.

items.title: Qedma Appoints Scott Aaronson to Its Scientific Advisory Board
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Qedma has appointed Professor Scott Aaronson, a leading quantum computing and computational complexity researcher, to its Scientific Advisory Board.

Aaronson will advise the company as it develops quantum error suppression and mitigation software aimed at improving the accuracy of quantum computations.

His research on quantum computational complexity and the evaluation of quantum advantage aligns with Qedma ‘s work on assessing the capabilities of quantum hardware.

PRESS RELEASE — Qedma , a quantum computing software company specializing in quantum error suppression and mitigation, today announced that Professor Scott Aaronson, one of the world’s leading researchers in quantum computing and computational complexity theory, has joined its Scientific Advisory Board.

Aaronson is the Schlumberger Centennial Chair of Computer Science at The University of Texas at Austin and Director of its Quantum Information Center. Internationally recognized for his pioneering contributions to quantum computing theory, his research has helped establish the theoretical foundations for understanding the capabilities and limitations of quantum computers, including what it takes to demonstrate quantum advantage over classical computing. In 2026, Aaronson was elected to the U.S. National Academy of Sciences in recognition of his contributions to scientific research.

His appointment brings deep theoretical expertise to Qedma as the company works to overcome one of the most significant barriers to practical quantum computing: errors and noise that limit the accuracy and scale of quantum computations.

items.title: PsiQuantum and AMD Expand Partnership on Quantum Computing Infrastructure
items.summary:
Insider Brief

PsiQuantum and AMD have expanded their strategic partnership to co-design the classical and quantum computing infrastructure required for utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum systems and hybrid applications.

The collaboration will extend beyond AMD Versal FPGAs to include Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs and the ROCm software stack, alongside PsiQuantum ’s silicon photonics platform, with AMD also planning an equity investment in PsiQuantum.

The companies will initially focus on pharmaceutical research and drug discovery, building on work involving GPU-based simulations of covalent inhibitors and a machine-learning decoder designed for real-time error correction.

PRESS RELEASE — PsiQuantum and AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced an expanded strategic partnership to co-design the computing infrastructure required to operate utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers and the hybrid applications that combine quantum, high-performance, and AI computing.

The collaboration builds on the companies’ existing work around AMD Versal FPGA technology—selected by PsiQuantum for the development of its fault-tolerant quantum computing platform—and expands it into a broader relationship spanning AMD Instinct GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, and the AMD ROCm software stack, combined with PsiQuantum’s silicon photonics platform and its fully integrated platform. As quantum systems scale toward practical use, PsiQuantum and AMD expect the integration of classical high-performance, AI, and photonic quantum computing technology to form the world’s most powerful hybrid computing fabric.

To reinforce its commitment to the partnership, AMD also plans to make an equity investment into PsiQuantum .

items.title: FAU Receives $3 Million Award for Quantum Workforce Development
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Florida Atlantic University (FAU) has received a $3 million U.S. Department of Labor award to develop quantum education and workforce training programmes focused on quantum sensing and communications.

The five-year initiative will establish educational pathways from early-college to graduate studies, with hands-on training using Rydberg-atom radio-frequency sensing equipment and an optical atomic clock supplied in collaboration with Infleqtion.

FAU expects the programme to reach more than 100 students and plans to use the new equipment to support research and training in quantum sensing and communications.

PRESS RELEASE — Florida Atlantic University ‘s Center for Connected Autonomy and Artificial Intelligence ( CA-AI ), within the College of Engineering and Computer Science , received a $3 million award from the U.S. Department of Labor’s Strengthening Institutions Program to develop a quantum-ready workforce in Florida through education and research training in quantum-enabled sensing and communications.

The project, “Building Florida’s Quantum-Ready Workforce: Quantum-Skilled Pathways in Integrated Sensing and Communications from Early College to Graduate Studies,” is led by George Sklivanitis , Ph.D., associate director of CA-AI, Charles E. Schmidt Associate Research Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and fellow of the Institute for Smarter Cities, Spaces, and Health; and Dimitris Pados , Ph.D., director of CA-AI, Charles E. Schmidt Eminent Scholar in Engineering, professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, and fellow of the Institute for Smarter Cities, Spaces, and Health.

The initiative will establish educational pathways that introduce students to quantum technologies beginning at the early-college level and continuing through graduate education. The program will combine foundational quantum education with advanced coursework and hands-on research work and training in quantum sensing and communications, preparing students with skills applicable to emerging quantum technologies.

items.title: Improved Low-Cost Quantum Error Mitigation with Benchmarked-Noise Zero-Noise Extrapolation (bnZNE)
items.summary:
We theoretically extend and experimentally demonstrate benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation (bnZNE), a simple and low-cost method for quantum error mitigation which aims to outperform the highly popular ZNE method for an equal total shot cost by improving the classical extrapolation step. We recently proposed bnZNE as a new error mitigation method (Harris et al., arXiv:2603.10224 (2026)) and showed that it can mitigate noise to the same order as standard ZNE under gate-wise depolarizing noise.

Here, we introduce randomized bnZNE which addresses the case of running multiple random circuits per noise level, allowing for the incorporation of noise-tailoring techniques like Pauli twirling and readout error mitigation, and test the method on the IBM and IQM hardware for a plethora of large-scale applications, observing bnZNE to consistently produce more accurate results than standard ZNE. Our approach enhances the extrapolation process to the zero-noise limit by using classically-simulable and structure-mirroring benchmark circuits, generated from the standard application circuit, to sensitively measure the effective error rate at each scaled noise level beyond simple integer values.

We give a new method for generating tailored benchmark circuits for the IQM superconducting devices and test them experimentally. Our results demonstrate that bnZNE presents a versatile alternative to ZNE which can enable more accurate results at utility scales with an equivalent cost.

items.title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off
items.summary:
General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity.

We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters.

Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens.

We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.

In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.

items.title: Stability Conditions on Twisted Derived Categories I: Existence and Full Numerical Support
items.summary:
We prove that for every nonempty smooth projective variety $X$ over an arbitrary field and every Brauer class $α$, the twisted derived category $D^b(X,α)$ admits a Bridgeland stability condition with full numerical support.

Based on Chunyi Li's construction and its extension to arbitrary fields, we establish uniform phase control under tensoring by an Azumaya algebra and calibrate the resulting slicing to the induced central charge.

We further show that the constructed stability condition is geometric and satisfies a mass--Hom bound, which persists throughout its connected component.

items.title: Communication Supremacy of a Qubit in Holevo Frenkel Weiner Scenario
items.summary:
The prevailing wisdom asserts that in the Holevo Frenkel Weiner (HFW) framework of communication tasks, a qubit offers no advantage over a c bit unless additional quantum resources are supplied or the classical shared randomness (SR) is restricted. In contrast, we establish the supremacy of qubit communication in the HFW framework when additional quantum resources, such as entanglement or measurement incompatibility are not injected and SR is a free resource.

We consider a prepare-measure scenario where the sender, Alice, prepares six states subject to a specific cryptographic constraint, and the receiver, Bob, performs a three-outcome measurement. Such a constraint on preparation impacts the power of qubit communication quite differently than that of c-bit communication, ultimately giving rise to the quantum advantage.

We introduce a witness capable of distinguishing quantum strategies that lie beyond the set of possible classical strategies and demonstrate the optimal quantum advantage. {As an application, we demonstrate the generation of certified randomness without requiring any seed randomness, since Bob has no input.} We further analyse the robustness of the witness and show that the advantage persists in noisy situations, making it suitable for experimental realisation. Finally, we demonstrate that Bob's three outcome qubit positive operator valued-measure (POVMs) has a distinct capability of detecting coherence, which can be regarded as the non-classical feature responsible for showcasing the quantum advantage.

items.title: Rohrbach's Conjecture for Finite Groups
items.summary: Rohrbach's conjecture holds for finite groups. In fact, there is an absolute constant $C$ such that, for every finite group $G$, every positive integer $h$, and all nonnegative real numbers $α_1,\ldots,α_h$ with $α_1+\cdots+α_h=1$, there are subsets $A_1,\ldots,A_h\subseteq G$ satisfying \[ G=A_1\cdots A_h, \qquad |A_1|\leq |G|^{α_1}, \qquad |A_i|\leq C|G|^{α_i}\quad(2\leq i\leq h). \] Consequently, for every $h$ there is a constant $c_h$ such that every finite group $G$ has a subset $A$ with \[ A^h=G\qquad\text{and}\qquad |A|\leq c_h|G|^{1/h}. \]

items.title: Quantum Elements Helps Rigetti Predict Quantum Hardware Behavior
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Rigetti Computing is using Quantum Elements ’ Constellation platform to simulate quantum processor behavior and assess how its systems will perform at scale.

Rigetti said three years of collaboration validated Constellation’s ability to predict single- and two-qubit gate performance on its 36-qubit and 108-qubit processors.

Constellation now supports Rigetti ’s quantum error correction pipeline by supplying inputs for noise models used to predict logical error rates.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Elements , developers of software that shortens the path to fault-tolerant quantum computing, announces that Rigetti Computing , a pioneer in full-stack quantum-classical computing, is leveraging Quantum Elements ’ Constellation platform to model quantum device behavior to better understand how systems will perform at scale.

Constellation gives quantum teams a development environment for running high-fidelity dynamic simulations. Physically accurate quantum digital twins running on classical computers enable teams to design, test, and analyze quantum systems before committing to hardware experiments. Constellation provides this capability by modeling the physical behavior of specific quantum processors.

“ Quantum Elements ’ Constellation platform has expanded our ability to model gate operations beyond few-qubit systems and understand the error channels that limit their performance,” said Dr. Subodh Kulkarni, CEO of Rigetti . “Through three years of collaboration, we have validated the platform’s ability to accurately predict single- and two-qubit gate performance on our 36-qubit and 108-qubit QPUs. Constellation is now part of our quantum error correction pipeline, providing inputs for the noise models we use to predict logical error rates.”

items.title: Chern characteristic classes of normal bundles of complex generalized flag submanifolds in generalized flag manifolds
items.summary:
We study Chern characteristic classes of normal vector bundles of complex generalized flag submanifolds $G_{n-1}/P_{n-1}$ in complex generalized flag manifolds $G_n/P_n$.

This procedure can be regarded as the relative version of Schubert calculus for the pair $G_{n-1}/P_{n-1}$ and $G_n/P_n$.

The CW structure and additive structure of the cohomology of $\mathrm{Gr}(n, k)$ allows inductive calculation of Chern classes of the canonical and complementary canonical vector bundles over $\mathrm{Gr}(n, k)$.

The combination of representation theory and algebraic geometry allows to derive analogous properties for the isotropic Grassmannians $\mathrm{LGr}(m, k)$ and $\mathrm{OGr}(m, k)$ via their embeddings in $\mathrm{Gr}(m, k)$.

Then the induced CW structure yields the additive structure on the cohomology of $\mathrm{LGr}(m, k)$ and $\mathrm{OGr}(m, k)$, and consequently leads to the calculation of Chern classes of the canonical and complementary canonical vector bundles over $\mathrm{LGr}(m, k)$ and $\mathrm{OGr}(m, k)$.

items.title: Integrals over Hilbert schemes and multiple $q$-zeta values
items.summary:
We establish a version of Okounkov's conjecture on multiple $q$-zeta values arising from integrals over Hilbert schemes of points on smooth projective surfaces.

We prove that normalized generating series of integrals involving products of Chern characters of tautological bundles belong to the algebra $\mathcal Z_q$ of multiple $q$-zeta values, without restrictions on the canonical class of the surface.

The proof combines vertex-operator methods with a reduction to graph sums, whose arithmetic structure is governed by the cohomology of the surface.

We also derive a closed universal formula for the Chern character operators acting on the cohomology of Hilbert schemes by solving a system of differential equations arising from Lehn's commutator relations.

items.title: Q-CTRL Secures US$290 Million Series C Funding Led by Salesforce Ventures
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Q-CTRL raised US$290 million in a Series C round led by Salesforce Ventures , achieving unicorn status and funding further expansion of its quantum software business.

The company develops AI-powered software for quantum computing and sensing, including its Ironstone Opal navigation system designed to operate without GPS.

Q-CTRL plans to expand globally, strengthen its software capabilities and scale customer programs across finance, energy, autonomy and aerospace.

Image: (From left) Robert Love, Chief Technology Officer; Michael Hush, Chief Scientist; and Michael Biercuk, founder and Chief Executive Officer, all of Q-CTRL .

PRESS RELEASE — Q-CTRL , the global leader in quantum infrastructure software, today announced a landmark Series C private fundraise of US$290 million (A$415 million), led by Salesforce Ventures . The round is headlined by significant participation from Bullhound Capital and Affinity Partners, and a global syndicate of new and existing investors.

The oversubscribed round mints the newest quantum-sector unicorn and places Q-CTRL among the best-capitalized quantum firms in private markets. The company’s Series C saw two expansions to meet investor demand and represents the largest quantum-sector fundraise for a software-focused business.

items.title: Reduced filtering using classical control hierarchy with linear optimality for continuous quantum error correction
items.summary:
Continuous quantum error correction promises reduced thresholds and hardware overhead compared to the digital paradigm, but its complex model estimation has greatly reduced its practicality. We recast this problem as a classical control-theoretic state hierarchy made of an exact bilinear reduced model, an exact conditional filter, and standard estimation and feedback design.

For any $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code whose generators are all continuously monitored and which is driven by a single Pauli recovery channel, we prove that the exact filter closes at dimension $3\cdot2^{\,n-k-1}$. This dimension is set by the syndrome space instead of the Hilbert space and is minimal within invariant-subspace filtering.

The reduced model exposes and corrects two failure mechanisms of the feedback loop. Strong monitoring damps the rotational partner through which the controller steers the stabilizer and injects back-action diffusion along the recovery path; lowering the measurement strength during correction raises the entanglement fidelity of partner-steering LQR control by $0.096$ in the three-qubit code with three monitored parities.

Linearizing at the codespace leaves the syndrome uncontrollable, so the controller can stall; a gain designed at a shifted operating point removes this degeneracy. In the limit of zero measurement during correction, we prove that a syndrome-only filter is exact at every recovery boundary.

The resulting committed-recovery controller needs only $2^{\,n-k}$ class probabilities and gives the highest entanglement fidelity compared among the methods tested in the literature, $0.947$ against $0.920$ for a measurement-based estimator protocol in the three-qubit bit-flip code, and $0.726$ vs at most $0.407$ for continuous controllers in the five-qubit perfect code.

items.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
items.summary:
Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture.

MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability.

A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction.

Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers.

These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.

items.title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
Speculative decoding accelerates text generation with large language models by letting a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large verifier checks in a single forward pass. We introduce Olifant, a draft model built on a memory-based classifier.

It predicts the next token from a four-token window in under 0.3 ms on CPU, requiring no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. We measure throughput and energy under two verifier regimes on consumer hardware.

Without a KV cache, drafting is nearly free: a domain-matched Olifant model reaches 38.1% acceptance on EU legal text, delivering 2.43x throughput and 2.51x lower energy per token than the neural verifier model alone. With a KV-cached verifier, itself a ~10x energy saver, drafting costs matter: a TinyLlama draft model halves throughput and triples energy despite high acceptance, whereas Olifant still yields 1.25x throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens, 14x below the uncached baseline).

We further show that KV caching decouples time from energy: verification of longer drafts raises power draw, shifting the energy-optimal draft length below the speed-optimal one. Speculative decoding is not dead in the age of fast verifiers, provided drafting is nearly free.

items.title: Residual Entanglement vs. Residual Coherence: A Wave Packet Approach in Neutrino Oscillation with Matter
items.summary:
In this work, we investigate quantum correlations in three-flavor neutrino oscillations beyond the standard plane-wave (PW) description by employing a wave-packet formalism in the presence of constant matter density. We study three quantum correlation measures, namely the residual $l_1$-norm coherence, Concurrence Fill, and Three-$π$ entanglement, and express them in terms of transition probabilities for an initial muon-flavor state.

The analysis is performed for the DUNE setup and extended beyond its baseline to study the interplay between wave-packet decoherence and matter effects over long distances. For the DUNE baseline, finite wave-packet widths suppress and smooth the oscillations relative to the PW case, with smaller widths causing stronger damping, while matter effects modify the amplitudes and positions of the oscillation features.

Among the considered measures, residual $l_1$-norm coherence dominates over the entanglement measures. At very long propagation distances, wave-packet decoherence progressively washes out the oscillatory behavior, driving the oscillation probabilities and quantum correlation measures toward averaged values, with smaller wave-packet widths leading to earlier damping.

Further, in the $L-δ_{\rm CP}$ plane, residual $l_1$-norm coherence exhibits weak $δ_{\rm CP}$ dependence, while Concurrence Fill and Three-$π$ entanglement show greater sensitivity at the DUNE baseline. Beyond a characteristic baseline in the extended propagation regime, all three measures approach constant values, independent of $L$ and $δ_{\rm CP}$.

items.title: Persistent-mediator architecture for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation with color codes
items.summary:
Two-dimensional color codes provide transversal Clifford gates, whereas suitable three-dimensional codes provide a transversal $T$ gate. Representative cross-dimensional schemes either switch the computational encoding or consume a 3D encoded state.

Reusing the same protected 3D block would remove repeated auxiliary-state preparation and terminal readout, raising a central question: can the 3D module remain encoded and protected while mediating successive $T$ gates on a separate 2D register? Here we introduce a cross-dimensional persistent-mediator architecture that retains the 2D data register and 3D mediator as distinct encoded modules at each cycle boundary, coupled only through a transient protected subsystem.

We construct a membrane-like joint-logical measurement and combine it with a matched cross-dimensional $CZ$, complementary string-like surgery, and feed-forward to close a deterministic logical $T$-gate cycle. The cycle avoids post-selection and destructive mediator readout and restores the 3D block to its initial logical state.

Stabilizer analysis establishes the logical action and preserved spatial distance. Phenomenological and circuit-level simulations of a Clifford surrogate show finite-distance scaling close to the matched 3D memory benchmark, while sequential tests show approximately linear logical-error accumulation in the low-error regime.

Persistent mediation enables repeated access to higher-dimensional non-Clifford capability while keeping the computational register in its 2D encoding.

items.title: Immaculate complexes and Strong Generation by Injectives
items.summary:
We study the category of bounded complexes of finite sums of indecomposable injectives over a locally Noetherian scheme, which we call the immaculate complexes. We show that regularity and finiteness of dimension can be detected from this category using strong generation.

Our methods involve studying when the unbounded derived category of a Grothendieck category is strongly generated by injectives. As applications we prove a conjecture of Hartshorne and recover a result of Keller and Krause.

To any specialisation closed subset we associate a semi-orthogonal decomposition of the immaculates and use this to compute additive finitary invariants in terms of the completions of the local rings. The immaculates are equivalent to the perfect derived category of a left coherent preadditive category i.e. a ring with many objects and we compute this category for one-dimensional integral or Gorenstein schemes.

items.title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
items.summary:
Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch.

For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load.

Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations.

Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.

items.title: A Quantum Algorithm for Computing All Eigenvalues and Eigenstates of Sparse Hermitian Matrices
items.summary:
Computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a sparse Hermitian matrix is a fundamental problem in algebra, arising both as a problem of independent interest and as a key subroutine in a wide range of computational and scientific applications. In this work, we develop a quantum algorithm that determines the spectrum of a sparse Hermitian matrix, defined as the set of its distinct eigenvalues, and for each eigenvalue, prepares a corresponding eigenvector as a quantum state in its eigenspace.

The eigenvalues are represented as binary strings with a prescribed precision, while the corresponding eigenvectors are kept as quantum states, eliminating the need to reconstruct their classical counterparts. The algorithm instead enables estimation of expectation values $\braket{x|M|x}$, where $\ket{x}$ is a prepared eigenstate and $M$ is an observable.

For an $n \times n$ $s$-sparse Hermitian matrix $H$, dense methods based on Householder tridiagonalization and QR iteration compute all eigenvalues and eigenvectors in $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ time. Exploiting sparsity, the Lanczos method computes all eigenvalues in $\mathcal{O}(n^2 s)$ time in exact arithmetic, but recovering all eigenvectors still requires $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ time.

In contrast, our algorithm runs in time $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n s^2 \log^2 n / Δ_{\min})$, where $Δ_{\min}$ denotes the minimum spectral gap of the normalized matrix. For inverse gaps up to $Δ_{\min}^{-1} = \mathcal{O}(n)$, the most favorable scaling for $n$ distinct eigenvalues, attained by nearly uniformly spaced spectra such as those of perfect-state-transfer spin chains and the Sylvester-Kac matrix, and for sparsity up to $s = o(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$, the proposed algorithm achieves an improved asymptotic runtime over the classical $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ approach for computing all eigenvalues and eigenvectors, under standard sparse-access assumptions.

items.title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor
items.summary:
The identification of heavy-flavor jets, i.e. collimated streams of particles originating from the fragmentation of beauty and charm quarks produced in proton-proton collisions, represents one of the most challenging classification tasks in measurements at Large Hadron Collider experiments. In recent years, advanced machine learning techniques have been successfully employed to address this problem, while quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative approach.

However, the high dimensionality of the problem, typically involving hundreds of observables, raises an open question: whether the current generation of quantum computers, characterized by limited qubit count, can effectively tackle such complex tasks. In this work, a variational quantum circuit for the classification of b- and c-jets at the LHCb experiment is implemented on a 5-qubit superconducting quantum computer manufactured by IQM and installed at the Politecnico di Torino.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a quantum algorithm for jet identification using simulated data from an LHC experiment in which all stages of the machine-learning workflow, including training and testing, are performed on real quantum hardware. The results demonstrate that the impact of hardware-induced quantum noise does not significantly degrade the performance.

A framework for the evaluation of the training time on the quantum hardware and for the circuit optimization is also proposed. These findings pave the way for future applications on larger quantum devices based on superconducting qubits, featuring a larger number of qubits enabling the encoding of information beyond the reach of classical simulation and providing a step toward investigating whether quantum advantage may eventually be achievable in high-energy physics classification tasks.

items.title: Gatemon qubits based on in-situ ternary InAsSb/Al nanowire Josephson junctions
items.summary:
Ternary InAsSb/Al nanowires combine compositionally engineerable semiconductor properties with epitaxial proximity superconductivity, making them attractive for hybrid quantum circuits and mesoscopic superconductivity. Here, we realize gatemon qubits based on shadow-defined in-situ InAsSb/Al Josephson junctions in a single growth process.

Gate-dependent microwave spectroscopy demonstrates electrostatic tuning of the qubit transition over several gigahertz. Rabi oscillations and Ramsey interference show coherent qubit control, with representative values T1 = 0.79 us and T2* = 0.91 us.

Across five gatemons distributed over three chips, the measured relaxation times range from approximately 0.2 us to 1 us and decrease with increasing qubit frequency. Their magnitude is comparable to a circuit estimate of spontaneous emission into the electromagnetic environment.

These results establish in-situ InAsSb/Al junctions as coherent, gate-tunable circuit elements and introduce cQED architecture as a microwave probe of the dynamics of the ternary weak link.

items.title: Qunova’s Hybrid Computing Method Matches Classical Benchmark for Iron-Sulfur Cluster
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Qunova Computing reported that its HI-VQE algorithm reached chemical accuracy in an 80-qubit simulation of an iron-sulfur cluster using an IBM quantum computer and RIKEN ’s Fugaku supercomputer.

The workflow’s extrapolated ground-state energy estimate agreed within chemical accuracy with a leading classical benchmark calculated using the Density Matrix Renormalization Group method.

In an intermediate calculation, HI-VQE used approximately 300 times fewer Fugaku node-hours than a previously published sample-based quantum diagonalization approach.

PRESS RELEASE — Qunova Computing , a world leader in quantum computations for advanced chemistry, today announces that it s HI-VQE algorithm has become the first quantum algorithm to reach chemical accuracy (a level of precision required for practical use) at 80 qubits. It did so while simulating the 4Fe-4S iron-sulfur cubane cluster in a quantum / classical super compute workflow using an IBM Quantum System Two quantum computer at RIKEN , along with RIKEN’s classical supercomputer Fugaku. This result represents the most accurate quantum computation of the molecule to date.

Qunova ’s extrapolation of the cluster’s ground-state energy, −327.2482 ± 0.0007 Hartree, is consistent within chemical accuracy regarding the leading classical reference calculated using the Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) method (−327.2471 Hartree).  This result is more accurate than the latest extrapolated Trimmed Configuration Interaction (TrimCI) results. This places a quantum-based approach on equal footing, in terms of accuracy, with the strongest classical methods available today for one of the most demanding problems in chemistry.

“ 4Fe-4S has long been a proving ground where only the very best classical methods could compete, and today a quantum algorithm has reached that standard,” said Kevin Rhee, CEO and founder of Qunova Computing . “Our ground-state energy estimate is within chemical accuracy with respect to the classical benchmark DMRG,  making HI-VQE the first quantum approach to achieve this type of result at this scale. We are also very encouraged that our method points to a slightly lower estimate of the groundstate energy estimate of the true ground state. Our next goal is to identify additional industrial use cases where HI-VQE consistently delivers better results than the best classical methods. We believe this result shows we are on the right path.”

items.title: Noise-Protected Superconducting Qudits from Higher-Harmonic Josephson Junctions
items.summary:
Qudits, which generalize qubits to $d$ levels, store more information per circuit element than qubits. As with qubits, however, their sensitivity to noise must be overcome before they can be used for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Here we show that, by exploiting the second harmonic of the current--phase relation, a superconducting loop of three Josephson junctions can host qutrits strongly protected against relaxation, while dephasing limits their coherence. When the second harmonic is positive, a simple loop with a small asymmetry between the junctions provides a tunable, symmetry-protected qutrit.

When it is negative, a protected qutrit can be realized by adding a small symmetry-breaking term, such as a weak Josephson diode effect. The two designs involve different trade-offs: the first has an exact charge selection rule, whereas the second is nearly insensitive to charge noise and its quasiparticle errors can be corrected.

The preferable choice therefore depends on the materials used. Both require a sizable second harmonic to begin with, and we identify altermagnetic Josephson junctions as a candidate platform.

Finally, microscopic calculations show that a gate voltage selects the sign of the second harmonic in these junctions, although gate-voltage noise then becomes the leading source of dephasing. These findings establish the sign of the second harmonic as a design principle for protected superconducting qudits.

items.title: SignRot: LLM Quantization with Massive Outlier-Aware Sign-Adjusted Rotation
items.summary:
While quantization compresses LLMs and accelerates inference, outlier activations impede efficient low-bit representation. In particular, massive outliers cause substantial performance degradation. Although rotation-based methods that rely on randomized Hadamard transforms for online inference aim to mitigate this, they can produce fragmented distributions with empty bins when a massive outlier dominates a token's activation.

This fragmentation severely undermines uniform quantization performance. Moreover, massive outliers concentrate in the down-projection input, where the preceding nonlinearity requires the rotation to be applied at inference time. This constraint prevents training-based approaches such as SpinQuant from learning the online rotation at this position, as a learned dense matrix cannot use the Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform and would require a full matrix multiplication during inference.

To address this, we propose SignRot (Sign-adjusted Rotation), which identifies massive outlier channels and constructs a sign adjustment vector that unifies the signs of the corresponding Hadamard row, collapsing the bimodal distribution into a unimodal profile amenable to quantization. Since the aligned outlier shifts the activation mean away from zero, we pair SignRot with asymmetric activation quantization, whose zero-point absorbs this shift. As a lightweight, drop-in improvement compatible with any Hadamard-based quantization method, SignRot requires only a single calibration forward pass and adds only element-wise sign flips at inference, without an additional matrix multiplication.

Applying SignRot to QuaRot achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 5.88 and an average zero-shot reasoning accuracy of 72.73, surpassing SpinQuant on the LLaMA3-70B model. Code is available at https://github.com/HYU-ARK-Lab/SignRot.

items.title: Quantum Mpemba effect from logical-information exposure in monitored circuits
items.summary:
In the Mpemba effect, a state initially farther from stationarity overtakes one that starts closer. After one cycle in a monitored Clifford chain, an unencoded Bell-pair state has lower mean entanglement entropy than a scrambled reference prepared from fewer pairs.

The gap grows linearly with chain length. This reversal is driven by logical-information exposure: a stabilizer state loses one ebit per independent logical parity resolved by the record.

Scrambling within each half can spread this information over many sites while preserving every Schmidt coefficient. We prove that with independent exact unitary two-design encoders, any pure reference ensemble with no greater mean initial entropy can lead in mean entropy by at most two ebits at any time.

If the stationary entropy is subextensive, the unencoded reversal is a quantum Mpemba effect at large sizes. We further certify this effect at 128 and 256 qubits using stationary-entropy bounds.

items.title: One Model, Two Precisions: Does Disagreement Between Quantized Copies Tell You When a Small Model Is Wrong?
items.summary:
Local language models often exist at several precisions, and quantization is known to change individual answers. This study asks whether the disagreement between two precisions of the same weights, an 8-bit copy that answers and a lower-precision copy that reads the same prompt, works as a per-question error score for abstention, escalation and re-asking. The cost is one extra forward pass over fewer bytes, with no sampling and no training.

We simulate round-to-nearest quantization with per-group scales (3 to 6 bits, groups of 32 to 256) on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B and score 8,398 multiple-choice questions from ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag subsets. Error detection is measured by AUROC, risk-coverage curves and ECE on a held-out half, with paired bootstrap intervals over questions. For Qwen3-0.6B, the entropy of the 8-bit answer reaches AUROC 0.682; the best disagreement score, selected on a development half, reaches 0.684 (+0.001 [-0.009, +0.011]), and combining it with the confidence features adds +0.009 [+0.002, +0.015], mostly on ARC.

On Qwen3-1.7B the selected score is -0.001 [-0.009, +0.006] from entropy and the combination +0.003 [-0.001, +0.006] on the test half. Gaussian weight noise at matched error energy is about as informative as rounding (0.6B only), so we find no evidence that the signal is specific to quantization, and shuffling the features within task and entropy cells removes the gain. One extra 8-bit pass that shifts the option order does better (+0.049 [+0.031, +0.067] over entropy) at about a third more weight traffic; routing to a larger model on free entropy beats both extra-pass scores at equal total traffic.

After logistic recalibration the 0.6B confidences are calibrated within a few points of ECE. A deployment recipe and the cases where the method does not help are given.

items.title: CyberRisk Collaborative Announces Virtual Event on Post-Quantum Readiness
items.summary:
Insider Brief

CyberRisk Collaborative has announced a virtual event, Post-Quantum Readiness: Preparing for Q-Day, scheduled for January 26, 2027, to examine the security and technology implications of quantum computing.

The programme will bring together cybersecurity, technology and cryptography leaders to discuss cryptographic risk assessments, post-quantum migration planning, crypto-agility and enterprise readiness.

Confirmed speakers include representatives from the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, SAP, Georgia Tech, Citi and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital, with sessions available on demand after the event.

PRESS RELEASE — CyberRisk Collaborative , a membership organization for senior cybersecurity leaders, today announced Post-Quantum Readiness: Preparing for Q-Day, a virtual event taking place Tuesday, Jan. 26, 2027, focused on the security, risk, and technology implications of advances in quantum computing.

The program will bring together cybersecurity and technology leaders to examine how organizations can assess their exposure to quantum-related cryptographic risk and begin preparing a transition to post-quantum security.

Quantum computing has the potential to undermine widely used public-key cryptographic systems that protect sensitive data, identities, infrastructure, software, and digital transactions. While the timeline for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer remains uncertain, large enterprises are increasingly evaluating the potential impact on long-lived data, critical systems, cryptographic dependencies, and future technology investments.

items.title: Circuit-Level Analysis of Quantum Error Correction in Second-Generation Quantum Repeaters
items.summary:
We present a circuit-level simulation of second-generation quantum repeaters with stabilizer-based quantum error correction. We model a two-segment repeater link including encoding, syndrome extraction, decoding, and entanglement swapping, and compare the performance of the single-error-correcting Steane and five-qubit stabilizer codes under different noise scenarios.

To that extent, we consider noise sources with incoherent (depolarizing and dephasing) and coherent (systematic over-rotation) errors and incorporate them directly at the circuit level. While the Steane code outperforms the five-qubit code at coherent errors, the five-qubit code achieves higher end-to-end fidelities under incoherent noise in the low-noise regime when a large number of physical qubits is affected by it.

At higher noise regimes, employing no code turns out to be the best option. In mixed noise scenarios, we observe moderate cross-effects between the noise classes regarding the error correction performance.

We conclude that code selection in second-generation quantum repeaters must be adapted to the dominant physical noise mechanism and that circuit complexity and hardware-aware implementation options influence performance in coherent-error-dominated regimes, providing design insights for error correction in quantum repeaters.

items.title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization
items.summary:
Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled.

Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity.

We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs.

Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.

items.title: Exact Quantum Algorithms for Composed Boolean Functions
items.summary:
We study exact quantum algorithms for block compositions of total Boolean functions. For an outer function $f$ of degree $D$ and an inner function $g$ on $m$ bits, we prove $$

Q_E(f\circ g)=O\!\left(mD+Q_E(f)Q_{1/(4D)}(g)\right). $$ The algorithm combines approximate inner evaluations with a finite exact correction. Its two costs are governed by different parameters of the outer function: exact query complexity determines the cost of simulation, whereas polynomial degree determines the number of inner blocks used in the correction.

We first establish the construction with an arity-dependent error threshold and then obtain the degree-dependent threshold above. For recursive ternary not-all-equal, this gives an exact algorithm using $(3/\sqrt2)^{k(1+o(1))}$ queries asymptotically. More generally, for every fixed nonconstant total gadget $h$, we determine the exact recursive rate as $\max\{\textrm{deg}(h),\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(h)\}$ and prove $Q_E(h^{\circ k})=\widetilde O_h(R(h^{\circ k})^2)$.

The composition limit also allows to transfer separations from $Q_{\varepsilon}$ and $°$ to exact quantum query complexity $Q_E$ (similar to fractional block sensitivity to block sensitivity transfer in Tal and Kulkarni 2016, Chicago Journal of Theoretical Computer Science). We construct a family with $s=\operatorname{bs}=\operatorname{fbs}\ge Q_E^{3/2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $1.1527\ldots$. A second construction gives $R \ge Q_E^{2-o(1)}$, improving the previous exponent $3/2$. We also allow different inner functions and give analogous quantitative separations in quantum communication.

items.title: Loss of the quadratic speedup in Grover search under local and coherent noise
items.summary:
Grover's algorithm searches an unstructured database with a number of oracle queries that grows only as the square root of its size. Noise erodes this advantage, and we ask, analytically, how quickly. When a depolarizing channel acts on the whole register after every gate layer, it commutes with the gates, and the noisy state is the noiseless one with a coherent weight that decays geometrically with depth.

The Grover rotation is not slowed. Its weight decays, the best stopping point moves earlier, and the expected query cost keeps its square-root scaling only while the accumulated noise over the circuit stays small. For independent errors on the qubits we show that the ideal Grover operator freezes any amplitude pushed out of the two-dimensional search plane.

This gives the exact effect of a single error: phase flips do most damage early in the search, bit flips late, and combined errors at any time. For large databases it also reduces the noisy search to Bloch-type equations for the part of the state that stays in the plane, in which the algorithm is a rotation and the noise appears as leakage and dephasing. We derive the rates for bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise and solve the equations.

Local noise acts, to leading order, like a global channel strengthened by the number of qubits, so the tolerable error per qubit falls faster than the inverse square root of the database size by one power of the register size. For coherent errors in the rotation angle we bound the success probability by a band that widens linearly with depth. Our results recover, in closed form, scalings found earlier for particular noise models, and they explain why some errors are more harmful than others.

items.title: Training quantum neural networks one job at a time
items.summary:
When a quantum processor is reached through a cloud queue, a variational algorithm pays for every round trip, and a single round trip can carry many circuits. The classical optimizer therefore decides how much is learned per job, not only per shot. We study this for a quantum neural network classifier.

We compare optimizers that are given the same number of jobs and the same shots per job, and that differ only in how they fill each job. This comparison treats hybrid quantum-classical training as an execution-efficiency problem: how to obtain useful optimization progress from each costly interaction with a quantum processor. The resulting perspective connects optimizer design to overhead amortization and efficient use of accelerator resources.

A direct port of a batched pattern search that worked for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm stalls once the model has a few dozen parameters. What does transfer is the principle behind it: fill each job with a batch of parameter vectors that is fixed before the job is sent. For circuits built from Pauli rotations the natural batch is the parameter-shift stencil.

We show that its gradient error falls as the inverse of the shots per job, while the error of simultaneous-perturbation methods (SPSA) has a floor that no number of shots removes. In simulation, batched parameter-shift training needs between a fifth and a half of the jobs SPSA needs, for 24 to 48 parameters, and the ordering holds at two noise levels. A new structure-aware stencil search reads the same kind of rows as sinusoids and also beats SPSA.

On IBM's ibm_fez processor, in three interleaved runs at six and eight qubits, the batched optimizer reached SPSA's final training loss within 4 to 20 of its 50 jobs. Its test accuracy was clearly higher at eight qubits; at six qubits the difference was not significant. All hardware numbers can be re-derived from the raw shots.

items.title: On the $h$-polynomials of cyclotomic standard graded Cohen-Macaulay rings
items.summary:
We say that a standard graded algebra is cyclotomic if all roots of its $h$-polynomial lie on the complex unit circle.

We study which products of cyclotomic polynomials can occur as $h$-polynomials of standard graded Cohen--Macaulay algebras without being of complete intersection type.

For each fixed positive integer $a$, we reduce the nonexistence problem for multiplicities $ap$ over all sufficiently large primes $p$ to finitely many cases.

Combining this reduction with explicit constructions, we completely characterize the positive integers $k$ for which such a polynomial of multiplicity $8k$ exists: precisely those satisfying \[k\notin\{1,2,3,6\}\cup\{p:p\ge7\text{ is prime}\}\cup\{3p:p\ge17\text{ is prime}\}.\]

items.title: Climate Temporal Temperature Prediction via an Adaptive Stacked Bidirectional Residual Mamba Network
items.summary:
Accurate temperatures forecasting relies on traditional meteorological parameters that are essential for monitoring weather informatics and guiding forecasting efforts. This study presents Deep DualMamba, a novel deep learning framework for temporal temperature prediction, built upon an enhanced variant of the recently proposed Mamba network.

Unlike conventional Transformer-based architectures, which dominate foundation models but suffer from computational inefficiencies on long sequences, Deep DualMamba leverages selective structured state space models (SSMs) to achieve both scalability and performance. We identify a core limitation of prior subquadratic-time models-namely, their inability to perform long-term and robust forecasting and introduce two key innovations.

First, we propose an adaptive bidirectional Mamba as encoders to learn complex and efficient features. Second, we develop a hardware-aware, parallel recurrent algorithm to compensate for the loss of convolutional efficiency, ensuring practical viability at scale.

Last, the Deep DualMamba's approximation ability and convergence is theoretical analyzed. These design choices culminate in a simplified, attention- and MLP-free neural architecture that exhibits linear complexity with sequence length and significantly improved inference throughput.

To demonstrate its applicability in climate informatics, we implement a full forecasting pipeline using historical meteorological data from UK monitoring stations.

items.title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
items.summary:
Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that can keep up with syndrome data streams and supply correction information and logical measurement outcomes to the quantum control system. Meeting these requirements at scale requires high throughput while controlling the end-to-end latency from readout to usable correction.

In this paper, we organize decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and code constructions using common classifications and examine their performance and trade-offs under the reported evaluation conditions. We distinguish decoder-level hierarchy, where multiple decoding stages or resources cooperate to decode a single code, from code-level hierarchy, where the code construction itself introduces multiple decoding levels.

We first review single-code hierarchical decoders and their cascaded predecoding and windowed, streaming, and distributed implementations. We then study hierarchical and concatenated codes, focusing on how decoding is coordinated across code levels through hard decisions, soft reliability information, or syndrome information.

We also examine how qubit modalities shape decoding workloads and timing requirements, and review how different decoding platforms meet these requirements, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), and cryogenic platforms. By assessing design trade-offs, this paper clarifies connections across the literature and provides a shared foundation for QEC design exploration.

It also identifies gaps in performance reporting and system integration to guide future research toward practical quantum error correction.

items.title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch
items.summary:
The quantum switch applies two operations in a coherent superposition of their causal orders and is a simple example of indefinite causal order. No quantum circuit that uses each operation once in a definite order can even describe it, yet photonic experiments have demonstrated its physical realization. We ask how many calls to the black-box operations a quantum computer in the circuit model needs to reproduce the switch.

If one of the black boxes is known to be unitary, three calls suffice. For general channels on a $d$-dimensional system, we prove three results. In all three, circuits may use classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary quantum memory.

First, no finite number of calls suffices for exact simulation in the worst case. Second, approximation to any fixed error below $1/2$, measured in half the diamond norm, requires $Ω(d^{1/4})$ calls, exponential in the number of qubits. Third, an ordinary circuit can require exponentially many calls to obtain a single bit that the switch extracts with a few uses.

We consider a device whose actual noise is dephasing in a fixed unknown basis and test it against a theoretical depolarizing model. The two channels have the same entanglement and average gate fidelities, so these figures alone do not distinguish them. At fixed noise strength, the quantum switch tells them apart with a number of device uses independent of $d$, whereas the circuit model requires $Ω(d^{1/16})$ calls.

Noise characterization is needed for quantum error correction, and this gives a provable query advantage of the switch in a task relevant to practical quantum computing. We invite future work that extends such advantages to more practical computing tasks.

items.title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
items.summary:
